title: Broad prevention of severe acute kidney injury

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a safe intervention or coordinated prevention strategy that reliably protects kidney function across substantially different causes of acute kidney injury and multiple high-risk care settings. Its intended scope includes injury associated with sepsis, major surgery, impaired circulation and toxic exposures. These are the settings identified in the supplied research; the review had no inspectable source material with which to independently verify that causal background or establish the full field-wide prevention gap.

The central capability would be dependable protection before severe injury develops, without requiring perfect advance identification of every patient who will be affected. A coherent strategy could involve several coordinated measures rather than a single treatment. Success in a selected surgical population would establish a useful but narrower capability than reproducible protection across different mechanisms and settings. Broad prevention does not require complete prevention in every patient.

significance.text: Conditional significance: preventing most severe acute kidney injury across several major high-risk settings would substantially shift kidney care toward protecting organ function before severe damage develops. The transformative feature would be the breadth and reliability of protection, extending beyond an isolated benefit in one patient population. This is a reasoned assessment of the proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

A reduction in episodes requiring kidney replacement therapy would be an important direct clinical outcome to test. Fewer moderate or severe injury episodes would not, by themselves, establish fewer kidney replacement episodes, less subsequent chronic kidney disease or improved survival. Those downstream benefits remain conditional and require their own outcome measurements and follow-up.

The proposed shift toward prevention has practical limits. A strategy that depends on narrowly selected patients, unusually intensive monitoring or resources unavailable in many hospitals might have substantial local value while falling short of broad protection. Likewise, success against one pathway of injury would not establish comparable effects against other causes. These are implications of the concept's scope rather than documented limitations of a particular intervention.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability, as framed by the research, is reliable protection across heterogeneous injury mechanisms and care settings with tolerable harms. The scientific challenge is to establish whether one protective approach can work across those differences, or whether a coordinated set of approaches can deliver comparably dependable results. The supplied review did not have sufficient documentary evidence to establish that this capability remains unavailable throughout the field.

Engineering and implementation barriers inferred from this goal include identifying patients early enough to intervene, delivering preventive measures consistently during changing clinical conditions, and retaining benefit when prediction is imperfect. A strategy must also accommodate different causes and patient circumstances without introducing unacceptable harm. These are proposed development challenges; the supplied material does not identify a validated universal mechanism or a specific technical solution.

A further barrier is demonstrating that protection extends beyond a short-term injury endpoint to outcomes that matter clinically. The development program would need to distinguish effects on injury severity, kidney replacement therapy, longer-term kidney function and survival. It would also need to separate the contribution of patient selection from the effectiveness and feasibility of the preventive strategy itself.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Zarbock and colleagues' BigpAK-2 report, described as published online in The Lancet on November 13, 2025, as a multinational randomized trial of a preventive care bundle in biomarker-enriched, high-risk patients after major surgery. It reports moderate or severe acute kidney injury within 72 hours in 14.4% of the intervention group versus 22.3% of controls. These quantitative details are retained as reported findings, not independently verified results: the source index contains the article citation and PDF URL, but no captured artifact or inspectable source text was available to the review.

If confirmed from the publication, that result would establish meaningful preventive benefit in the studied surgical population and early postoperative period. It would not establish protection across sepsis, toxic exposures or other substantially different settings. The supplied research also attributes a limitation to the report: the trial was not powered to detect changes in long-term outcomes. Because the underlying passage was not available for inspection, that limitation remains an attributed description; it nevertheless gives no basis for assuming long-term kidney or survival benefits.

The evidence boundary is document access and verification. The review could not inspect the publication's identity, completeness, methods or supporting passages, and the quotation supplied with the candidate was not independently inspected evidence. That limitation does not show that the reported trial or result is false. Separately, no bounded freshness assessment was supplied for developments through November 1, 2026, so the record cannot establish how the field evolved after the dated report or whether it represents the latest evidence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized trials across several substantially different high-risk settings should show a large, reproducible reduction in moderate or severe acute kidney injury, together with benefit on prespecified clinically consequential kidney outcomes and acceptable safety. The settings should test the intended breadth of protection rather than repeatedly examine closely similar surgical populations. This is a proposed evaluation framework, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Trials show large moderate-to-severe AKI reductions across distinct high-risk settings

completion_criteria.text: Before testing, investigators should define what counts as a large benefit, acceptable harm and a clinically consequential outcome. Kidney replacement therapy should be measured directly if a reduction in its use is claimed. Longer follow-up should assess kidney function and survival, with any claims about chronic kidney disease or mortality supported by trials designed and powered to evaluate those outcomes.
completion_criteria.label: Benefit, harm and consequential outcome criteria defined before testing

completion_criteria.text: Reproducibility should include independent confirmation and implementation across varied hospitals, patient groups and resource conditions. Evaluation should document how patients are selected, how consistently the strategy is delivered, and where its benefits or safety limits change. Finite trials can establish demonstrated breadth across the settings tested; they cannot establish literal universality. Complete prevention in every setting is neither assumed feasible nor required by this proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Independent confirmation across varied care conditions documents benefit and safety limits

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with NEP-01, Regrow functional nephrons inside an adult human kidney, and NEP-02, Rebuild function in scarred kidneys by reversing established fibrosis: all concern preserving or restoring native kidney function. NEP-10 focuses on preventing severe acute injury, whereas NEP-01 proposes creating functional nephron tissue and NEP-02 addresses established scarring. Prevention would not itself demonstrate regeneration or reversal of fibrosis.

Conceptual comparison with NEP-03, Manufacture transplantable human kidneys from cells; NEP-04, A durable, implantable artificial kidney; NEP-05, Kidney replacement that is portable and affordable at global scale; and NEP-06, An effectively unlimited supply of durable animal-donor kidneys: these concepts address replacing kidney function or expanding replacement capacity. NEP-10 aims to avert acute loss of function. Successful prevention could reduce some demand for replacement, but it would not resolve the need for replacement among patients whose injury is not prevented or whose kidney failure has other causes.

Conceptual comparison with NEP-07, Reliably induce donor-specific tolerance in kidney recipients: its defining capability is immune acceptance of a donor kidney. NEP-10 instead concerns protection against severe acute injury across causes and settings. Their clinical domains could intersect in transplant recipients, but evidence of acute injury prevention would not demonstrate donor-specific tolerance, or vice versa.

Conceptual comparison with NEP-08, A root-cause, durable treatment for ADPKD, and NEP-09, Durable reversal of diabetic kidney disease: these target particular underlying diseases and durable changes in their course. NEP-10 targets acute injury across different causes. Shared goals of preserving kidney function do not make disease modification, reversal of chronic disease and broad acute injury prevention interchangeable capabilities.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record lacks captured source text needed to verify the BigpAK-2 publication, trial design, biomarker selection, endpoint, numerical results and stated long-term power limitation.
The listed causes of acute kidney injury and the field-wide absence of broad, reliable prevention were not independently supported by inspectable documentary evidence in the supplied review.
Developments through November 1, 2026 were not assessed in a supplied freshness record; the dated trial report cannot establish the latest state of the field.
The intervention or coordinated strategy capable of delivering broad protection remains unspecified, including how it would work when advance risk identification is imperfect.
The proposed criteria require operational definitions of benefit magnitude, acceptable safety, outcome selection, follow-up duration and sufficient diversity of settings.
Whether broad prevention would reduce kidney replacement therapy, subsequent chronic kidney disease or mortality remains a question for direct testing.

brief.title: Reliable protection against sudden kidney damage
possible: People facing major surgery, severe infection, poor circulation or toxic exposures could receive care that protects their kidneys before severe damage develops. Protection would work across different causes, even when doctors cannot perfectly predict who will be affected.
This could come from a treatment or several coordinated care measures. The goal is dependable protection across different hospital settings.
why: For patients at high risk, this would shift kidney care toward preserving function before severe damage occurs. Its value would come from protection that extends across different illnesses and procedures.

sources.showed: BigpAK-2 is a multinational randomized trial of coordinated preventive care in selected patients at high risk of kidney injury after major surgery.
sources.cited_for: It supports preventive care after major surgery in selected patients.
sources.not_established: It does not establish protection across different causes of kidney injury or long-term benefits.

sources.who: Giovanni Landoni and the PROTECTION Study Group
sources.showed: Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, given through a drip reduced sudden kidney injury after heart surgery. The trial also found fewer cases of the most severe injury.
sources.quote:
Among adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery, infusion of amino acids reduced 
the occurrence of AKI.
sources.cited_for: It shows that a preventive treatment can reduce kidney injury in a defined surgical setting.
sources.not_established: It does not establish broad protection or fewer patients needing treatment that replaces kidney function.

sources.who: Simon Finfer and the PLUS Study Investigators
sources.showed: In critically ill adults, a fluid with salts balanced more like those in blood did not lower kidney injury or death compared with ordinary salt solution.
sources.quote:
We found no evidence that the risk of death or acute kidney injury among criti -
cally ill adults in the ICU was lower with the use of BMES than with saline.
sources.cited_for: It shows that changing the fluid used in intensive care did not provide the hoped-for kidney protection.
sources.not_established: It does not rule out other preventive treatments or coordinated care strategies.

sources.who: Steven D. Weisbord and the PRESERVE Trial Group
sources.showed: After imaging of blood vessels, sodium bicarbonate given through a drip offered no benefit over salt solution. The drug acetylcysteine offered no benefit over a dummy treatment in preventing kidney injury or the combined outcome of death, dialysis or lasting kidney decline.
sources.quote:
There were no significant between-group differences in the rates of con-
trast-associated acute kidney injury.
sources.cited_for: It shows that widely used preventive approaches failed in another high-risk setting.
sources.not_established: It does not establish an effective alternative or protection across other causes of kidney injury.

shown: Landoni and the PROTECTION team reduced sudden kidney injury after heart surgery using amino acid drips. Zarbock and colleagues reported fewer moderate or severe injuries with coordinated care after major surgery. These are advances in surgical patients; protection across different causes remains to be demonstrated.
missing: Trials have yet to establish reliable, safe protection across substantially different causes and care settings.
A strategy has yet to show dependable benefit when advance identification of patients at risk is imperfect.
Broad prevention has yet to demonstrate fewer treatments replacing kidney function, less lasting kidney disease or better survival.

milestones.label: Large reductions across different high-risk settings
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials would have to show large, repeatable reductions in moderate or severe injury, meaningful kidney benefits and acceptable safety. This would establish protection beyond similar surgical populations.

milestones.label: Benefit and safety criteria defined before testing
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to define meaningful benefit and acceptable harm beforehand, measure claimed outcomes directly and follow kidney function and survival. This would distinguish early protection from lasting clinical benefit.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation across varied care conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to confirm benefit across hospitals, patient groups and resource levels, documenting patient selection, delivery and safety limits. This would establish how broadly the strategy works.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether broad protection needs a single treatment or several coordinated measures.
The required size of benefit, acceptable harms and sufficient variety of test settings still need definitions.
Whether preventing early injury also reduces lasting kidney disease or death remains open.

page.title: Prevention of moderate-to-severe acute kidney injury
page.definition: An intervention or coordinated care strategy reduces moderate or severe acute kidney injury (AKI) across major surgery, sepsis and nephrotoxic exposure in adults. Moderate and severe mean KDIGO stages 2 and 3, classified using blood creatinine, urine output or treatment that replaces kidney function.

goal.need: The International Society of Nephrology's 2015 commission estimated about 13.3 million AKI cases annually. It identifies injury severity and duration as affecting dialysis requirement, kidney recovery and survival. Prevention must therefore distinguish reductions in injury severity from separately demonstrated reductions in dialysis use or mortality.

statements.body: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, Renal Diagnostics and Therapeutics Unit
statements.quote: Our long-term goals are to find markers to detect AKI and to develop therapies to treat and prevent AKI.
We suggest using protocol-based management of hemodynamic and oxygenation parameters to prevent development or worsening of AKI
statements.context: Recommendation 3.1.3 addresses high-risk perioperative patients and patients with septic shock.

statements.body: 31st Acute Disease Quality Initiative consensus conference
statements.quote: Novel interventions for the prevention or treatment of acute kidney injury (AKI) are currently lacking.
statements.context: The conference developed recommendations for prevention and treatment trials, including AKI stage as a phase 3 prevention endpoint.

completion.title: A prevention strategy reduces stage 2–3 AKI across surgery, sepsis and nephrotoxic exposure.
completion.criterion: The same specified intervention or coordinated strategy reduces KDIGO stage 2–3 AKI versus usual care in randomized trials in each tracked setting. Each setting meets its trial's prespecified superiority criterion and safety requirements. Trials test the stage 2–3 endpoint directly, rather than infer it from biomarkers, all-stage AKI or a pooled effect across settings. Follow-up windows and statistical thresholds come from the registered protocols; no universal effect-size or harm margin is specified.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; a provisional cross-setting test assembled from published prevention goals and clinical endpoints.
completion.basis: Searches of KDIGO's 2012 guideline and March 2026 public-review draft, ADQI's 2024 trial consensus, regulator guidance and prize criteria found no published completion threshold for prevention across these settings. ADQI supports AKI stage as the clinical endpoint. Requiring setting-specific efficacy preserves the stated breadth without inventing a minimum percentage reduction.

milestones.title: A candidate reduces experimental AKI against injured animal controls at P<0.05.
milestones.criterion: A candidate reduces kidney dysfunction and tissue injury versus injured animal controls at P<0.05. In Doi et al.'s 2008 sepsis study, intravenous AP214 10 µg at 0 and 6 h, or starting 6 h after sepsis induction, reduced creatinine and tubular damage at 18 h. Creatinine experiments used 7–10 treated and 10–14 injured controls per group; histology used 6 treated and 8 injured controls. This is a study-specific proof of concept, not a validated predictor of human benefit.
milestones.set_by: Doi and colleagues, published experimental protocol approved by NIDDK's animal care and use committee. The test was written for a mouse sepsis model; it supplies a preclinical example, not a universal efficacy cutoff.
milestones.threshold_quote: The null hypothesis was rejected when P < 0.05.

milestones.title: A randomized human prevention trial reduces AKI within 72 hours at two-sided α=0.05.
milestones.criterion: A randomized human prevention study lowers its prespecified AKI endpoint. PrevAKI specified KDIGO AKI within 72 h and two-sided α=0.05: in 276 cardiac-surgery patients, AKI occurred in 76/138 receiving the care bundle versus 99/138 controls (P=0.004; 2017). In PRESERVE, bicarbonate versus saline and acetylcysteine versus placebo did not reduce contrast-associated AKI (4993 patients analysed; 2018). These results concern their studied populations and endpoint definitions.
milestones.set_by: PrevAKI investigators, registered study DRKS00006139 and published methods. The 72-hour test was written for cardiac surgery; protocols for other settings must specify their own observation window.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary endpoint was the occurrence of AKI within the first 72 h after cardiac surgery.

milestones.title: A multicentre prevention trial reduces stage 2–3 AKI at its prespecified confirmatory threshold.
milestones.criterion: A multicentre randomized study reduces stage 2–3 AKI at its prespecified confirmatory threshold. BigpAK-2 used a 72 h endpoint and adaptive testing with overall two-sided α=0.05: 1180 randomized, 1176 analysed; 84 (14.4%) versus 131 (22.3%) events (P=0.0002; 13 November 2025). PROTECTION (3511 adults; 2024) found stage 3 AKI in 29/1759 versus 52/1752, but kidney replacement in 24 versus 33. PLUS (5037 adults; 2022) found new kidney replacement in 306/2403 versus 310/2394. Those kidney-replacement comparisons did not establish benefit.
milestones.set_by: University Hospital Muenster, BigpAK-2, NCT04647396, statistical analysis plan dated 12 May 2023. Written for major surgery; the adaptive analysis controls overall one-sided error at 2.5% in each direction.
milestones.threshold_quote: The significance level of each of the one-sided tests will be 2.5%.

results.finding: In mice with surgically induced renal ischemia, alpha-MSH reduced kidney dysfunction and tissue injury (function: 21 treated, 18 controls; histology: 4 per group; P<0.05).
results.detail: The study used bilateral renal pedicle clamping as a surgical ischemia-reperfusion model. This is experimental proof of concept, not evidence of clinical benefit.
results.quote:
alpha-MSH significantly reduced
ischemia-induced renal damage, measured by changes in renal histology and plasma blood urea nitrogen and creatinine in mice.

results.finding: In cisplatin-treated mice, magnesium replacement reduced kidney dysfunction and tubular injury (4–5 mice/group for histology; P<0.001).
results.detail: Compared with magnesium-deficient cisplatin controls, replacement significantly reduced BUN, creatinine and tubular injury. Replacement began before cisplatin; the injured controls remained magnesium deficient.

results.finding: PrevAKI enrolled 276 cardiac-surgery patients; the care bundle reduced AKI within 72 hours by 16.6 percentage points.
results.detail: The prespecified primary endpoint was KDIGO AKI within 72 hours (P=0.004; two-sided α=0.05). The single-center trial enrolled biomarker-identified high-risk adults. Moderate-to-severe AKI was a secondary endpoint.
results.quote: In this randomized clinical trial of patients undergoing cardiac surgery, the implementation of a bundle of supportive measures in high risk patients identified by elevated biomarker levels reduced the occurrence of AKI within 72 h compared to standard care.

results.finding: In 292 high-risk contrast-exposed patients, AKI occurred in 16/146 with RenalGuard versus 30/146 controls (P=0.025).
results.detail: The prespecified primary endpoint was assessed at 48 hours. It included creatinine increases consistent with stage 1 AKI; the trial was not powered for dialysis or death.
results.quote:
Contrast-induced acute kidney
injury occurred in 16 of 146 patients in the RenalGuard group (11%) and in 30 of 146 patients in the control group
(20.5%; odds ratio, 0.47; 95% confidence interval, 0.24 to 0.92).

results.finding: In 501 patients undergoing coronary angiography or intervention, delayed remote ischaemic preconditioning reduced contrast-associated AKI (P = .03).
results.detail: The randomized trial reports a lower primary AKI endpoint, but the supplied text does not specify whether AKI was assessed within 72 hours or whether the P value was two-sided.
results.quote: The incidence of CA-AKI was 7.6% with sham and 3.2% with delayed RIPC (odds ratio 0.4, 95% confidence interval 0.17-0.94; P = .03).

results.finding: In 2,998 patients exposed to contrast, rosuvastatin reduced CI-AKI from 3.9% to 2.3% (P=0.01).
results.detail: The primary endpoint was assessed at 72 hours using the study's creatinine-based CI-AKI definition. It does not establish a reduction specifically in KDIGO stage 2 or 3 AKI.
results.quote:
The incidence of CI-AKI was lower in the rosuvastatin-
        treated group (2.3% vs. 3.9%, p ¼ 0.01) (Fig. 2).
